title: Content freshness and Query Deserves Freshness
summary: Google's ranking systems guide lists 'query deserves freshness' systems that show fresher content for queries where it would be expected, such as news about a recent earthquake. Google's How Search works page says factor weights vary by query and that freshness matters more for current news than for definitions. A 2011 post (old, so systems may have changed) names recent events, recurring events and frequently updated information. Google estimates byline dates from several factors; dates must reflect real publication or update.
actions: Decide per query whether freshness is expected before investing in updates.
Update pages when facts change, and show accurate visible dates plus dateModified.
Never stamp new dates onto unedited pages.

myths.myth: Every page needs regular updates to rank.
myths.correction: Google says freshness matters more for current news than for dictionary definitions, and weights vary by query.

myths.myth: Changing the date makes a page fresh.
myths.correction: Google says dates must describe the actual publication or update date and that it uses several factors to estimate it.

items.prompt: What does QDF stand for in Google's ranking systems guide wording? Give the phrase.
items.explanation: The guide says Google has various 'query deserves freshness' systems designed to show fresher content for queries where it would be expected.

items.prompt: Which example does Google's ranking systems guide give for freshness?
options: A. A sourdough bread recipe
B. A recent earthquake
C. A dictionary legal definition
D. A classic nineteenth-century poem
items.explanation: Correct: if an earthquake happened recently, news articles and fresher content might appear. Wrong: the other options (a recipe, a legal definition, an old poem) are not examples the guide gives.

items.prompt: True or false: Google's 2011 freshness post says the change noticeably impacts 6 - 10% of searches.
items.explanation: The post says the change noticeably impacts 6 - 10% of searches. It also says 'roughly 35 percent of searches'; the surrounding context was not saved.

items.prompt: Why does Google's How Search works page say freshness is not equally important for every query?
options: A. Weights vary by query; news needs freshness more
B. Freshness only applies to image results, never text
C. Old pages are always penalised by Google
D. Definitions need daily updates to rank
items.explanation: Google says, for example, that for current news topics content freshness plays a bigger role than dictionary definitions, and that the weight of each factor varies with the query. Wrong: 'Freshness only applies to image results, never text' - not stated. 'Old pages are always penalised by Google' - not stated. 'Definitions need daily updates to rank' - the quote says freshness plays a smaller role for dictionary definitions than for current news.

items.prompt: True or false: changing a page's date without changing its content is a sourced way to signal freshness.
items.explanation: Google says its systems look at several factors to estimate when a page was published or significantly updated, and that dates must describe the publication or update date of the page. A date edit alone does not describe an update (reasoned from the quote).

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the saved Google sources?
options: A. Google has query-deserves-freshness systems
B. Freshness matters more for current news than definitions
C. Google does not rely on one date factor
D. Every page must be updated monthly to keep rankings
items.explanation: Correct answer D: no saved source says pages must be updated monthly. Supported: A (guide: QDF systems), B (How Search works: news vs definitions), C (byline dates: Google does not depend on a single date factor).

items.prompt: The 2011 post names recent events, regularly recurring events, and frequently updated information as freshness cases. A query about the schedule of a yearly festival fits which case? Answer with one word: recent, recurring, or updated.
items.explanation: Events that take place on a regularly recurring basis are the post's second case. Mapping the festival query to it is the worked example.

items.prompt: A plan says: (A) show a visible date on articles; (B) use datePublished and dateModified accurately; (C) set every date to today on 400 unedited pages. Which step conflicts with Google's guidance?
options: A. Step A
B. Step B
C. Step C
D. None of them
items.explanation: Google says dates must describe the publication or update date of the page; stamping unedited pages with today's date does not. A matches Google's advice to add a user-visible date. B matches its recommendation to specify the datePublished and/or dateModified fields, when accurate.

items.prompt: Case file (hypothetical site, Northvale Tax Guides) combining intent with freshness: the team re-dates its evergreen 'What is a W-2?' page weekly while its page on this week's filing-rule change has not been touched in months. Evidence: (1) Google says freshness plays a bigger role for current news topics than for dictionary definitions; (2) the guide says QDF systems show fresher content for queries where it would be expected; (3) Broder defines informational intent as acquiring information assumed present on web pages. Which action is best?
options: A. Keep re-dating both pages every week
B. Remove dates from both of the pages
C. Update the rule-change page only
D. Merge both pages into one single page
items.explanation: Correct: apply the freshness effort to the time-sensitive query and stop date-bumping the definition page. The link between intent type and freshness need is practitioner inference; the two Google statements support it. Wrong: 'Keep re-dating both weekly' - effort on the wrong page. 'Remove dates everywhere' - Google advises a visible date. 'Merge both pages' - blends two different needs.

items.prompt: Case file (hypothetical site, Lakeside Reviews): a product review updated last week shows an old byline date in results. Evidence: (1) Google says a byline date is its estimate of when a page was updated or published; (2) Google says it does not depend on a single date factor; (3) the page shows no visible date and no dateModified. Which action is best?
options: A. Set a date in the future
B. Show a date; set dateModified
C. Do nothing and wait for a recrawl
D. Rely only on structured data dates
items.explanation: Correct: Google advises a prominent user-visible date and recommends specifying datePublished and/or dateModified. Wrong: 'Set a date in the future' - Google says not to specify future dates. 'Do nothing and wait for a recrawl' - ignores Google's advice and nothing saved says a recrawl fixes it. 'Rely only on structured data dates' - Google says it uses several factors, not one.
